2610.29762v1.accessible: Light, vibrations and similar physical systems behave like 'bosonic modes', which can hold many quanta of energy, whereas a qubit is a two-level system. To simulate such a mode on a quantum computer, it must be encoded into several qubits. Using simulations on ordinary computers, the authors compare three encodings, including a new one based on so-called Dicke states, by accuracy, number of qubits and number of operations. A compact binary encoding comes out best overall; the new encoding gives very short circuits but needs many more qubits. They also run two small test cases on a 56-qubit trapped-ion quantum computer, where noise visibly distorts the results. The authors stress that their comparison is far from comprehensive.
2610.29762v1.simple: Quantum computers use qubits. Some things in nature, like light, can hold many packets of energy. To study them on a quantum computer, you must spread each one over several qubits. The authors compare three ways to do this, mostly by simulating them on normal computers. One way uses few qubits and works well. A new way gives short programs but needs many qubits. A small test on a real quantum computer showed errors from noise.

2610.28185v1.accessible: When a black hole slowly evaporates, does the information about what fell in survive? This 'information paradox' has puzzled physicists for decades. Written from the philosophy of physics, this review analyses recent attempts to tackle it with the tools of quantum information theory, assuming evaporation loses no information. Here the black hole is modelled as a quantum circuit that scrambles information quickly and uses entanglement as a resource. The authors spell out the assumptions behind this approach and argue that it marks a real change in how physicists use the idea of 'information': as a practical modelling tool, rather than a measure of ignorance or a kind of substance. They argue that philosophers should pay more attention to it.
2610.28185v1.simple: Black holes can slowly disappear by giving off heat. Physicists ask: what happens to the things that fell in? Is that information lost forever? This is an old puzzle. New ideas treat a black hole like a quantum circuit that mixes up information very fast. In a review written from philosophy, the authors look closely at these ideas and what they assume. They say this way of thinking about information is useful. They think philosophers should study it more.

2610.20855v1.accessible: Moving a quantum state from one place to another inside a quantum computer is a basic task. Mathematicians can prove exactly which networks (graphs) of connected sites move a state from one end to the other with certainty, just by letting the system evolve, and at what time; for 'peak state transfer' the goal is the highest probability a network allows. The authors test this theory in experiments on IBM's 156-qubit Heron processor, deliberately without error correction or error mitigation, so the hardware's noise is part of the outcome. They cover several families of networks of growing size and compare with passing the state along step by step using swap operations.
2610.20855v1.simple: A quantum computer sometimes has to move information from one qubit to another. Some networks of qubits can do this perfectly, all by themselves, if you wait the right time. Mathematicians have proved which networks can do this. The authors test this on a real 156-qubit quantum computer from IBM. They use no error correction, so the machine's own noise shows up. They try several networks and compare with moving information step by step.

2610.17078v1.accessible: A network can be described by a single number, its 'spectral radius', which measures how well connected it is. This maths paper asks: if you remove one link of a network and add a new link elsewhere, keeping it connected, can you always do so without lowering that number? Networks where this is possible for every link are called 'sustainable'. The authors study this question for trees, networks without loops. They find infinite families of sustainable and non-sustainable trees, prove that a tree with one node linked to more than half of all nodes is never sustainable, and describe exactly which trees sit on the boundary. They end with open questions.
2610.17078v1.simple: This maths result is about trees: networks with no loops. One number tells how well a network hangs together. The authors ask a question: can you move any one link to a new place without making that number smaller? If yes, the tree is called 'sustainable'. They find many trees that are sustainable and many that are not. A tree with one point linked to over half of all points is never sustainable.

2610.11540v1.accessible: To gauge a quantum computer's quality, experimenters run random sequences of operations and see how fast the output quality decays: a method called randomized benchmarking. For realistic, structured circuits, the first part of this decay is distorted, so experimenters have to run long circuits, where the signal can drown in noise. This paper fixes this purely by processing the data differently. A new 'trace filter function' removes the distortion and gives reliable estimates from short circuits, with mathematical guarantees, at the price of more statistical scatter. Tests on a Rigetti superconducting processor, with circuits of up to 12 qubits, show it works with fewer than 10 layers of operations, where the standard method needs more than 40.
2610.11540v1.simple: People test quantum computers by running random steps and checking how fast mistakes build up. With some tests, the first results are misleading. So people run long tests, but then the signal gets lost in noise. The authors found a new way to look at the data. It gives good answers from short tests, though the answers scatter a bit more. They tried it on a real quantum computer with up to 12 qubits. Tests four times shorter were enough.

2610.06794v1.accessible: Gaussian states are a family of quantum states that appear everywhere in physics, for example in light and in electrons in materials. A natural question is how to check whether an unknown state is Gaussian or far from it. Earlier methods needed more copies of the state as the system got larger. The authors prove mathematically that a fixed number of copies is enough, no matter how large the system is, both for bosons (such as light) and for fermions (such as electrons). The proof uses the symmetry of identical copies and tools borrowed from the study of random walks on a sphere.
2610.06794v1.simple: Gaussian states are a common kind of quantum state. They show up in light and in electrons. Suppose someone gives you a quantum state. Is it Gaussian or not? To check, you need several copies of the state. Old methods needed more copies for bigger systems. The authors prove mathematically that a fixed small number of copies is always enough. This works for both light and electrons.

2610.06723v1.accessible: A basic law of quantum physics forbids perfectly copying an unknown quantum state, but from many copies one can make one extra, nearly perfect copy. How many copies are needed? For general states the answer is astronomically large. This theoretical paper shows it is far smaller when the state is known to belong to a structured family important in physics, such as Gaussian states of fermions (particles like electrons) or of bosons (such as light). For fermions the authors construct the best possible copying procedure, cutting the cost from exponential to polynomial in the system size. For bosons their method also has polynomial cost but is not always optimal. A separate construction gives optimal copying for 'phase states'.
2610.06723v1.simple: In quantum physics you cannot make a perfect copy of an unknown state. But from many copies, you can make one more that is almost perfect. How many copies do you need? Usually a huge number. Using maths, the authors prove that you need far fewer if the state is of a special, common type. For one type they find the best possible way to copy. For another, their method works but may not be the best.

2610.03714v1.accessible: Future large quantum computers will protect information with error-correcting codes, and every computation starts by preparing special encoded states without letting a single error spread. This paper presents SpiderCSS, software that automatically designs such state-preparation circuits for a broad family of codes (CSS codes). It uses the ZX-calculus, a graphical language for quantum circuits, and only applies rewriting steps that are known to keep the circuit fault-tolerant, so no costly checks are needed afterwards. In simulations with codes of distance up to 15, the circuits are smaller and shallower than those of existing methods, with on average 34% fewer logical errors.
2610.03714v1.simple: Big quantum computers will need to fix their own errors. For this, they store information in a special code. Before a computation, the computer must set up coded states without letting errors spread. The authors made a tool called SpiderCSS. It designs these set-up steps automatically. It uses a picture language for quantum circuits. In computer simulations, its designs are smaller and make about a third fewer errors than older methods.

2610.01979v1.accessible: A quantum state of many particles is a 'product state' if the particles are not entangled with each other. The authors design an efficient test, with a mathematical proof that it works, that decides whether an unknown state is close to a product state or far from all of them, using a number of copies that does not grow with the number of particles. The key idea is to randomly group the particles into a few blocks, which reduces the problem to a small number of parties. The same ideas give a much better algorithm for finding the product state that is closest to the unknown state.
2610.01979v1.simple: Particles can be entangled: they cannot be described one by one. A 'product state' has no entanglement at all. The authors design a test to check if a state is close to a product state, and prove that it works. The test needs only a fixed number of copies, even for very many particles. The trick is to put the particles into a few random groups. The same trick also helps to find the closest product state.

2609.40331v2.accessible: Linear threshold functions decide yes or no by checking on which side of a line (or, in higher dimensions, a plane) a data point lies; they are among the most basic tools in machine learning. The authors give three quantum algorithms for learning such functions, with proven bounds on their cost. If the learner may ask for the answer at any point it chooses, the quantum algorithm needs a number of questions that grows only logarithmically, whereas classical methods need a number growing with the dimension. For a special case related to majority voting, it improves an earlier quantum algorithm exponentially. A third algorithm works in a weaker setting, learning from quantum 'examples' instead of chosen questions.
2609.40331v2.simple: Many computer programs sort things into two groups with a simple rule: which side of a line is a point on? This is common in machine learning. The authors design three quantum methods to learn such a rule, and prove how well they work. In one setting, a quantum computer needs far fewer questions than a normal computer. In another, the new method beats the best earlier quantum method by a wide margin.

2609.40231v1.accessible: A classic problem is deciding whether two points in a network are connected. This paper studies a quantum version: each link of the network carries a quantum operation, and following a path from one point to the other transforms a quantum state along the way, in a way that does not depend on which path is taken. The task is to decide whether the two points are connected and, if so, how the transported state compares with a target state. The authors design a quantum algorithm that solves this in time roughly proportional to the number of points while using very little memory, and prove mathematically that no quantum algorithm can do substantially better.
2609.40231v1.simple: Are two points in a network linked by a path? This is a classic computer problem. In the quantum version studied here, each link changes a quantum state as it passes, and every route gives the same result. The task: are the two points linked, and what does the state look like after the trip? On paper, the authors design a fast quantum method that uses little memory. They also prove that no quantum method can do much better.

2609.40228v1.accessible: In 'non-local quantum computation', two parties who share entanglement try to apply a joint quantum operation to their inputs while exchanging messages only once, at the same time. This question matters for the security of quantum position verification, for communication complexity and even for quantum gravity. It was known that every operation can be done approximately with finite entanglement. The authors prove that doing it exactly is almost never possible: even for two qubits, almost every operation has no exact protocol with finite resources. The proof uses tools from geometry. Some simple, natural operations are also shown to be impossible to do exactly.
2609.40228v1.simple: Two people each hold part of a quantum system. They share some entanglement. They want to do a joint operation, but may only send each other one message at the same moment. Can they always do it perfectly? The authors prove mathematically: almost never, even for the smallest systems. They can only get close. This matters for checking where someone is with quantum signals, and for some ideas about gravity.

2609.40144v1.accessible: Extra qubits can make quantum circuits faster by giving them working space, but usually this space must start in a clean, known state. This paper asks whether 'dirty' qubits, already in use and possibly entangled with other parts of the computer, can serve instead, as long as they are returned exactly as they were. The authors prove that an important class of quantum circuits, Clifford circuits, can be run this way in very small depth, just as fast as with clean workspace. The price is a large number of borrowed qubits, growing roughly with the square of the circuit size. They extend the result to further families of quantum gates.
2609.40144v1.simple: Quantum computers can work faster if they have extra empty qubits to use as scratch paper. But usually that scratch paper must start out blank. The authors ask: can you borrow qubits that are already in use, as long as you give them back exactly as they were? They prove that for an important kind of quantum program, this works. The program runs just as fast as with blank scratch paper, but needs many borrowed qubits.

2609.40106v2.accessible: Quantum circuits can often be written in many different ways that do the same thing. A complete set of rewrite rules lets you turn any such version into any other, which is useful for simplifying and checking circuits automatically. This paper gives such a complete set of 16 simple rules for Clifford circuits, an important class, on qudits: quantum units with an odd prime number of levels instead of two. Each rule involves at most three qudits and has an intuitive meaning. The completeness proof was also checked by computer in the Agda proof assistant.
2609.40106v2.simple: The same quantum program can be written in many ways. The authors give 16 simple rules to turn one way of writing it into any other. This helps computers simplify and check quantum programs. The rules work for an important type of program, on quantum units with three, five, seven or another odd prime number of levels. Each rule is short and easy to understand. A computer has checked their proof.

2609.40080v1.accessible: Entanglement is a key resource for quantum communication, but in practice it is noisy. 'Distillation' turns many noisy entangled pairs into fewer, nearly perfect ones. The best possible rate depends on the exact noisy state, which is usually unknown. The authors design a universal procedure that first learns the state using only local operations and ordinary communication, then adapts its distillation. They prove that in the long run it reaches the same optimal rate as if the state had been known all along. They also find the best rate that works for a whole family of possible states at once.
2609.40080v1.simple: Entanglement is a special connection between quantum particles. It is useful for sending quantum messages, but real entanglement is often messy. You can turn many messy pairs into a few clean ones. This is called distillation. Usually you need to know exactly how messy the pairs are. The authors design a method that first learns this, then cleans the pairs. They prove that in the long run it works as well as if you had known everything.

2609.39980v1.accessible: In quantum error correction, information is spread over many qubits. Sometimes it is useful to move it back onto just one or a few qubits quickly, for example to send it onward through a network. 'Stabiliser path finding' does this with a single round of measurements on individual qubits, even when some qubits have been lost. Using ideas from percolation theory, the authors prove that for large surface codes, a widely used design, it succeeds almost surely as long as each qubit is lost with probability below one half. They also give two algorithms to find the right measurements, one exact and one much faster heuristic, and confirm the threshold in computer simulations.
2609.39980v1.simple: Quantum computers protect information by spreading it over many qubits. Sometimes you want it back on a few qubits, fast. A method called stabiliser path finding does this with one round of measurements. It works even if some qubits are lost. The authors prove that, for large codes of a common type, it almost always works if each qubit has less than a half chance of being lost. They also give a fast way to compute what to measure.

2609.39452v1.accessible: Simulating molecules is one proposed use of quantum computers, but accurate results normally need very large sets of basis functions, because electron wavefunctions have sharp features where electrons meet. The 'transcorrelated' method builds these features into the equations, so smaller basis sets suffice. The catch is that the resulting equations are non-Hermitian, which makes standard quantum algorithms harder to apply and their cost depend on how sensitive the solutions are. This theoretical paper studies this trade-off. In a solvable model, it shows that the faster convergence can improve the proven upper bound on the quantum algorithm's cost. It then extends the analysis to realistic electronic-structure equations.
2609.39452v1.simple: Quantum computers may one day help to study molecules. To get good answers, the calculation must handle places where two electrons come very close. This usually makes the calculation very big. A trick called the transcorrelated method makes it smaller. But the trick also makes the maths harder for quantum computers. The authors study this trade-off on paper. In a simplified model, they show that the trick can lower the expected cost of the quantum calculation.

2609.39280v1.accessible: Quantum tomography means learning an unknown quantum state or process from measurements, which in general needs very many copies. The authors show mathematically how to learn states and processes much more efficiently when they are known to have certain symmetries, and find the optimal number of copies or uses needed in several important cases. The trick is to reduce the task to estimating a pure state. Along the way they solve an open problem: they design efficient quantum circuits for the optimal measurement for pure-state estimation, by encoding states into modes like those of light and using a quantum version of the Hermite transform.
2609.39280v1.simple: Tomography means finding out what an unknown quantum state is by measuring it. This usually needs very many copies. The authors look at states and processes that have some symmetry. For these, they work out the smallest possible number of copies needed. They also solve an open problem: how to design an efficient quantum circuit for the best measurement. All of this is mathematical work, not a lab test.

2609.38091v2.accessible: Many problems in physics and chemistry come down to finding the lowest-energy state, the 'ground state', of a quantum system. Suppose you can already prepare a rough guess that overlaps somewhat with the true ground state, and you roughly know its energy. The authors prove how a quantum computer can then turn the guess into a very accurate ground state, using an optimal number of steps of the system's time evolution, up to a constant factor. They give two algorithms, one based on amplitude amplification and one based on 'transducers'. It completes their recent results on estimating ground-state energies.
2609.38091v2.simple: In physics and chemistry, people often want the state with the lowest energy. This is called the ground state. Suppose you already have a rough guess of it. The authors design a method for a quantum computer that turns this guess into a very good answer, and prove how well it works. Their method uses the smallest possible number of steps, up to a fixed factor. They give two ways to do it.

2609.28694v1.accessible: Polar molecules are candidate building blocks for quantum computers, but making two molecules interact quickly enough is hard. This paper proposes to use Rydberg atoms, atoms with one electron in a very large orbit, as fast go-betweens. By dressing the atoms with microwaves, unwanted interactions are switched off and the atom-molecule interaction is tuned just right, so that many pairs of molecules can be entangled at the same time. For sodium-caesium molecules with caesium atoms, the gate would be more than a hundred times faster than a direct gate between molecules. The scheme has not yet been built; the authors model its main error sources to give first estimates of gate quality, and show some errors can be detected afterwards.
2609.28694v1.simple: Small molecules could be used to build quantum computers. But it is hard to make two molecules work together fast. The authors suggest using helper atoms, with one electron pushed very far out, in between. Microwaves tune these helpers just right. Then many pairs of molecules could work together at once, over a hundred times faster than linking molecules directly. Some mistakes could be spotted afterwards. This is a design on paper, not yet built.

2609.28138v1.accessible: Trapped ions, charged atoms held by electric fields, are a leading platform for quantum computers, but their motion must first be cooled to very low energies. Standard 'Doppler' laser cooling leaves some motion behind, and the next step, 'sideband' cooling, works best on ions that are already cold. The authors propose a stage in between. A hollow, tightly focused laser beam (an optical tweezer) combined with microwaves makes the ion lose energy as it repeatedly climbs a hill, a trick called Sisyphus cooling. Addressing one ion cools the shared motion of small ytterbium crystals. So far it is studied only in simulation: with up to three ions, the joint motion cools in under two milliseconds.
2609.28138v1.simple: Ions are charged atoms. Scientists trap them to build quantum computers. First, the ions must be made very cold. Normal laser cooling stops at some point. Another method gets them colder, but it only works once they are already cold. The authors suggest a step in between. They shine a thin, hollow laser beam and microwaves on just one ion. Computer simulations with up to three ions show quick cooling. It has not yet been tried in a lab.

2608.27298v1.accessible: Quantum mechanics forbids making perfect copies of an unknown quantum state, but approximate copies are possible. The question is how many originals are needed to produce a given number of extra copies of good quality. For 'pure' states, which contain no added randomness, the best method has long been known. For 'mixed' states, which do contain randomness, a simple trick extends that method, and its cost grows with the state's 'rank', a measure of how mixed it is. The authors prove that no method can do better, so this simple approach is optimal. They show the same for approximate transposition, which turns copies of a state into copies of a mathematically 'transposed' version.
2608.27298v1.simple: In the quantum world, you cannot make a perfect copy of an unknown quantum state. But you can make rough copies if you start with several originals. How many originals do you need? For the simplest states, called pure states, the answer was known. For mixed states, which contain some randomness, there was a simple method. The authors prove mathematically that no method can beat it. They show the same for a related task that makes a flipped version.

2608.24493v2.accessible: A standard quantum computing task is estimating the 'ground-state energy', the lowest possible energy, of a physical system. A common approach starts from a 'guiding state', an initial guess that partly overlaps with the true lowest-energy state, and lets the system evolve in time. The key cost is the total evolution time needed. A faster method was found recently, but matching limits were known only in special cases. The authors prove that this method is optimal: no algorithm can do better in general, taking into account the accuracy wanted, the quality of the guess and the allowed chance of failure all at once. Similar limits hold for preparing the ground state itself and for several variants of the problem.
2608.24493v2.simple: Every physical system has a lowest energy. Quantum computers can estimate it if they start from a good guess. The work takes time, and faster is better. A fast method was found recently. The authors prove mathematically that no method can be faster in general. The limit depends on how good the guess is, how precise the answer must be and how sure we want to be. Similar limits hold for related tasks, such as preparing the lowest-energy state.

2608.18743v1.accessible: This technical proposal describes AICE, a 100-metre atom interferometer proposed for an access shaft of the Large Hadron Collider at CERN; it has not yet been built. An atom interferometer uses laser light to split clouds of very cold atoms into two paths and recombine them; tiny differences between the paths reveal faint forces. AICE's main goal is to search for 'ultralight dark matter', a hypothetical form of the invisible matter in the universe, in a mass range other experiments cannot reach. It would also pioneer the search for low-frequency gravitational waves and test Einstein's equivalence principle. The design uses ultracold strontium atoms. Studies found no technical showstoppers at the site.
2608.18743v1.simple: Scientists propose a new experiment at CERN called AICE. It has not been built yet. It would be about 100 metres tall, inside a deep shaft. In it, very cold atoms are split and joined again using lasers. This makes them very sensitive to tiny forces. The main goal is to look for a very light kind of dark matter. It could also look for gravitational waves. Studies found no technical obstacles at the site.

2607.27957v1.accessible: Entanglement is a form of correlation between quantum particles with no everyday counterpart. The authors design a task in which several separated senders each send a message to one receiver, and prove the following. If the senders share a special multi-party entangled state, called a GHZ state, each needs to send only a very small number of ordinary bits. Without shared entanglement, at least one sender must send far more, even if quantum messages are allowed. So ordinary messages plus shared entanglement can be exponentially more powerful than quantum messages alone. For cryptography, they build a 'randomness extractor', a tool for producing secure random bits, which shows a similar gap in the memory needed to break it.
2607.27957v1.simple: Entanglement is a special kind of connection between quantum particles. The authors design a task where several people each send a message to one receiver. They prove that if the senders share entangled particles, very short messages are enough. Without this, at least one sender must send much longer messages, even quantum ones. The authors also apply this to cryptography. There, a little shared entanglement greatly reduces the memory an attacker needs.

2607.11847v1.accessible: Learning a quantum state means measuring many copies of it to build a full description; the minimum number of copies needed is called the 'sample complexity'. Gaussian states are an important family of quantum states, both for bosons (such as particles of light) and for fermions (such as electrons). They are used across physics, chemistry and quantum computing, yet their sample complexity had not been fully worked out. The authors settle this question: in both cases the number of copies needed grows with the square of the number of 'modes', the independent parts of the system. This holds for pure and mixed states and needs no limit on the state's energy. The proof uses a generalised 'random purification' technique.
2607.11847v1.simple: To learn an unknown quantum state, you must measure many copies of it. How many copies are needed? For one important family, called Gaussian states, nobody knew for sure. These states appear in light, in chemistry and in quantum computers. The authors prove the answer mathematically. The number of copies grows with the square of the size of the system. This is true for both main kinds of particles and for any amount of energy.

2606.26354v2.accessible: In non-local quantum computation, two cooperating players who share entanglement, and may exchange only one simultaneous round of messages, try to carry out a quantum operation on a system split between them. This matters for quantum position-verification, which proves one's physical location cryptographically, and even quantum gravity. Such tasks are linked by 'reductions': a method for one task yields a method for another, which ranks their difficulty. The authors prove many new links in the most practical setting, with large classical and small quantum inputs. For example, simply redirecting a qubit based on a classical bit already enables many more complex operations. So many practical position-verification schemes have similar entanglement costs and hence similar security.
2606.26354v2.simple: Imagine two partners far apart who want to do a quantum task together. They share entangled particles and can each send one quick message. Such tasks help to check where someone really is, using quantum physics. The authors prove mathematically that many of these tasks are connected. If you can do a simple one, you can also do much harder ones. This means that many location-checking schemes are about equally secure.

2605.16494v1.accessible: In open quantum systems, which lose energy to their surroundings, some states are 'dark': they hardly decay at all. Such states are well understood for one or a few excitations, but their effect on many interacting particles is largely unexplored. The authors study theoretically a chain of spins (tiny quantum magnets) in which neighbouring sites lose energy together, creating a dark state for a single particle. They show that this state changes how the whole many-particle system behaves at long times. Through interactions with other modes, the dark state itself slowly decays, and the system follows universal patterns over time. The results help explain conflicting findings in recent work and are backed by computer simulations.
2605.16494v1.simple: Some quantum systems slowly lose energy to their surroundings. But certain states, called dark states, barely lose any. Using calculations, the authors study a chain of tiny quantum magnets that has one such dark state. They show that this dark state changes how the whole chain behaves over long times. The chain follows simple, general rules as it fades. Computer simulations agree. This helps explain why some earlier studies disagreed.

2605.00485v1.accessible: 'Entanglement entropy' measures how strongly two parts of a quantum system are entangled. Despite its name, it cannot directly drive heat flows, as ordinary thermodynamic entropy can. To do so, the entangled state must first become a random mixture through 'quantum state reduction', the collapse-like process associated with measurement. In a theoretical analysis, the authors show that, even in the simplest two-part system, entanglement entropy does not turn into thermodynamic entropy one-for-one. The random dynamics of state reduction also allow several definitions of entropy. They explain why this still forbids perpetual motion, and show that physical models of state reduction predict thermodynamic signatures distinguishable from the loss of quantum coherence caused by the environment.
2605.00485v1.simple: Two quantum particles can be entangled. Scientists measure how strongly with a number called entanglement entropy. But you cannot use it directly to make heat flow. First, the entanglement must be broken by a random process, like what happens in a measurement. Using theory, the authors show that this change is not one-to-one. They explain why it still cannot power a machine that runs forever. They also predict signs that experiments could look for.

2603.23628v3.accessible: Quantum theory forbids two seemingly useful operations: making perfect copies (cloning) of an unknown quantum state, and producing its 'transpose', a mathematically flipped version. The reasons differ: cloning clashes with linearity, transposition with 'complete positivity', a consistency rule for physical processes. The authors show that, despite this, the best possible approximations of both come from a single physical process: one output carries the best clone, the other, 'complementary', output the best transpose. Using this, they determine exactly how much quantum and private classical information the optimal cloning machine can transmit, closing an open gap. They give an explicit circuit doing both tasks equally well, prove that the optimal transposition is unique, and also study a mixed-state case.
2603.23628v3.simple: Quantum physics forbids making perfect copies of an unknown quantum state. It also forbids making a perfect flipped version of it. The two bans have different reasons. The authors prove that the best rough copy and the best rough flipped version come from one single process. This helps them answer an open question about how much information a copying machine can carry. They also design a circuit that does both tasks equally well.

2603.09580v1.accessible: The ZX-calculus is a graphical language in which quantum computations are drawn as diagrams and simplified with rewrite rules. To turn a diagram back into a runnable program, such as a circuit or a sequence of measurements, one needs a 'flow' condition guaranteeing that the computation is deterministic. Existing flow conditions require diagrams in a rigid special form, which ordinary rewrite rules easily break. The authors introduce ZX-flow, a condition stated directly in the ZX language using new markings called Pauli semiwebs. They prove ZX-flow survives all basic (Clifford) rewrites and matches an established condition, Pauli flow, up to such rewrites. Any diagram with ZX-flow can be read as a deterministic measurement-based computation or efficiently turned into a quantum circuit.
2603.09580v1.simple: Some scientists draw quantum programs as pictures, using a method called the ZX-calculus. They can change the pictures with simple rules to improve the programs. But in the end, the picture must turn back into a working program. Older checks for this only work on pictures with a strict shape. The authors give a new, more flexible check. It keeps working when the picture is changed. Pictures that pass can be turned into working quantum programs.

2602.13099v3.accessible: A 'k-design' is a finite set of states that mimics a truly random choice up to a certain level of detail, k. Welch bounds, inequalities first found in signal processing, tell exactly when a set is a perfect design. The authors prove stronger Welch bounds that measure how close a set comes to being a design; this characterises approximate designs. The bounds are often tight, which identifies the best approximate designs among small sets. For example, complete sets of 'mutually unbiased bases', a well-known structure in quantum theory, turn out to be optimal in this sense. This leads to a new numerical approach to whether such sets exist in dimension six, which the authors explore.
2602.13099v3.simple: Many quantum tasks need a set of states that behaves as if picked at random. The authors prove better ways to measure how close a small set comes to this ideal. With these tools, they can spot the best possible small sets. One famous family of sets turns out to be among the best. This gives a new way to search for such sets with computers, which the authors try out in one case.

2601.22981v1.accessible: Light carries 'spin', linked to its polarisation, which can couple to its motion. In the optical Magnus effect, this coupling shifts sideways the place where light acts most strongly, in a direction that depends on its spin. The authors directly observe and map this effect, using a single trapped calcium ion as a tiny probe. With a tightly focused laser beam, the spot where the ion interacts most strongly with the light moves sideways by several hundred nanometres. This comes from parts of the light's electric field that point along the beam, which appear only in a tight focus. The results matter for controlling atoms and ions with focused light, as in optical tweezers.
2601.22981v1.simple: Light can carry a kind of spin, linked to how it is polarised. When a laser beam is focused very tightly, the spot where it acts most strongly on an atom shifts a little to the side. The direction of the shift depends on the light's spin. In a lab experiment, the authors see this shift directly, using one trapped charged atom. The shift is less than a thousandth of a millimetre. This matters for controlling atoms with focused light.

2601.16564v3.accessible: Neutral atoms are promising for quantum computers because many can be arranged and connected flexibly. The authors built and describe an apparatus that holds single strontium atoms in a 5 by 5 grid of 'optical tweezers', tightly focused laser beams that each trap one atom. Atoms leave a custom-built oven, are slowed and guided into an ultra-high-vacuum chamber, and are cooled by two laser stages to a few millionths of a degree above absolute zero. The tweezers load atoms at random, so not every site is filled, and the atoms can be imaged very reliably, almost always surviving. The machine is intended as the core of a full quantum computer aimed at quantum chemistry problems.
2601.16564v3.simple: Quantum computers can be built from single atoms. The authors built a machine that holds strontium atoms with laser beams. Each beam, called a tweezer, holds one atom. There are 25 tweezers in a 5 by 5 grid, though they fill at random. The atoms are cooled with lasers until extremely cold. The machine can then photograph each atom, almost without losing any. It is meant to become the heart of a quantum computer for chemistry.

2608.28573v2.accessible: The quantum Fourier transform is a basic building block of many quantum algorithms, used to reveal hidden structure linked to symmetries. For simple, 'commutative' symmetry groups (called abelian groups), efficient circuits for it are known. For more complicated, non-commutative (non-abelian) groups, efficient constructions exist for only a few families. The authors develop two new mathematical methods for designing these circuits, based on Mackey theory and Clifford theory. With them they construct exponentially cheaper circuits for specific families of groups, including a family of matrix groups and so-called wreath products, where they remove a size restriction needed by earlier general methods. Together, the methods give systematic tools for many finite groups.
2608.28573v2.simple: Many quantum algorithms use a step called the quantum Fourier transform. It helps find hidden patterns linked to symmetry. For simple kinds of symmetry, we know how to do this step fast. For more complex kinds, we often do not. Using maths, the authors give two new recipes for building this step on a quantum computer. For some families of complex symmetries, their recipes are much cheaper than before. The recipes also cover many other cases.

2608.26282v1.accessible: The holographic principle says that what happens inside a region of space can be described by information on its boundary, a bit like a hologram. Starting from 't Hooft's original formulation, this philosophy-of-physics paper examines the role of 'information' in quantum gravity, the attempt to unite quantum theory and gravity. The authors identify three roles: limits on how much information a region can hold help select viable theories; the inside and boundary descriptions must carry the same physical content; and the way information is encoded links to current ideas in which space emerges from patterns of entanglement. They argue that everyday or Shannon-style notions of information fall short here, and call for a more systematic philosophical treatment.
2608.26282v1.simple: Physicists try to join quantum physics and gravity. One idea, called holography, says that what happens inside a region of space can be fully described on its edge. The authors, writing from philosophy, look at what 'information' means in this idea. They find it plays three roles. It helps rule out theories, it links two descriptions of the same thing, and it ties space to quantum links. They say the usual idea of information is not enough here.

2608.24370v1.accessible: Ordinary computers can simulate quantum circuits, but this becomes hard when circuits contain 'non-Clifford' gates, the ingredients that make quantum circuits difficult to imitate. Many new simulation methods have appeared, using techniques such as stabiliser decompositions or tensor contraction, and each works better for some kinds of circuits than for others. The problem is that every paper tests its method in its own way, on its own circuits and on its own hardware, so results are hard to compare. The authors present ABSTRACTS, a standard benchmark suite: a fixed collection of test circuits together with consistent (virtual) hardware and supporting infrastructure, so that different simulators can be compared fairly.
2608.24370v1.simple: Scientists often use normal computers to imitate quantum computers. Many new methods for this have appeared. But each team tests its method in its own way, on its own test cases and its own machines. This makes it hard to know which method is best. The authors build a shared test set. It has a fixed list of quantum circuits and the same virtual machines for everyone. This allows fair comparisons between methods.

2608.18650v1.accessible: Truly random quantum operations are too costly to build, so researchers use unitary designs: collections of circuits that imitate randomness well enough, up to a chosen level of detail. The authors construct such designs for qubits arranged in a line (1D), where gates act only on neighbours. They prove that their circuits are nearly as shallow as possible and use nearly the smallest possible number of 'magic' gates, the costly gates needed beyond the easier Clifford gates. They match known lower bounds in all parameters at once, up to a small factor, by refining and combining two earlier constructions. As a by-product, they give a small fixed set of local 1D circuits that generates the whole Clifford group.
2608.18650v1.simple: Many quantum tasks need operations that look random. Making truly random ones is too expensive. So scientists design circuits that are 'random enough'. The authors do this on paper for qubits sitting in a line, where each step only touches neighbours. They prove their circuits are almost as short as possible. They also use almost the fewest costly 'magic' steps possible. They get this by improving two older methods and joining them together.

2607.24712v2.accessible: Some quantum states are valuable 'resources', for example because they are entangled or contain 'magic', a property needed for powerful quantum computation. Resource testing asks how reliably one can tell such a state apart from all resource-free states, given many copies of it. A recent result, the Generalised Quantum Stein's Lemma, describes how fast the errors shrink, but only in the limit of infinitely many copies, so it gives no guarantee for any real, finite number. The authors prove the first rigorous bounds for a finite number of copies, with explicit estimates of how many are needed. As consequences, they settle an open problem about certain entropy measures and give the first bound of its kind on the copies required.
2607.24712v2.simple: Some quantum states are useful, like fuel for quantum computers. Scientists want to test if a state is really useful. They look at many copies of it. An older result says how well this works with endless copies. But real labs only have a limited number. Using maths, the authors give the first firm guarantees for a finite number of copies. This says how many copies you need. It also solves an open maths question.

2607.11483v1.accessible: Quantum circuits can model how physical systems change in discrete time steps. In a theoretical study, the authors analyse circuits whose gates come from a supersymmetric quantum field theory in one space and one time dimension. Arranged in a 'brick-wall' pattern, these circuits support strong zero modes: special quantities that stay conserved as the system evolves. How many there are depends on the circuit parameters. Some stay at the edges of the system, while others travel steadily through it, steered by the parameters; a particular interaction term in the dynamics explains this motion. The authors describe how the travelling modes could transport quantum information and discuss how robust this would be to noise.
2607.11483v1.simple: Quantum circuits can imitate how nature changes step by step. On paper, the authors look at circuits built from parts taken from a theory of particles with a special symmetry. In these circuits, some quantities never change over time. Some stay at the edges. Others move through the circuit at a steady speed. The settings steer them. The authors explain how these moving quantities could carry quantum information, and how well this would cope with noise.

2606.25037v2.accessible: Quantum position verification aims to check where someone is located without trusting them, using quantum signals. It faces two obstacles: attackers who share entanglement (quantum correlations between particles) could cheat, and in experiments many photons are lost on the way. An earlier 'commitment' trick tackles both, but its proof only works when the protocol is repeated round after round. With a different proof, the authors show security when all rounds are run at once, in parallel, against attackers with limited entanglement. The protocol tolerates any amount of photon loss and noise up to 3.7%, so loss no longer limits the verification distance. They also correct and strengthen the earlier analysis of the round-by-round version.
2606.25037v2.simple: Can you check where someone is without trusting them? Quantum position checking tries to do this with light signals. But cheaters who share entangled particles could fool it, and light often gets lost on the way. An older trick fixed both problems, but only when the test runs one round at a time. The authors prove it also works when all rounds happen at once, if cheaters have limited entanglement. Then any amount of lost light is fine.

2605.07518v1.accessible: The standard quantum circuit model treats every quantum algorithm as a straight-line program: a fixed list of steps. This makes it awkward to run subroutines of different lengths in superposition, a quantum combination of several branches of a program. Quantum walks, an alternative way to describe quantum algorithms, can model such branching. Applied to Grover's search algorithm, however, branching alone gives a variable-time search that is worse than earlier results. The authors trace this to a second feature of real programs that was missing: loops. By extending the method to handle looping as well, they match the complexity of previous work. This shows the importance of modelling a program's control flow properly when designing quantum algorithms.
2605.07518v1.simple: A quantum algorithm is usually written as a fixed list of steps, one after another. But real programs have branches and loops, and some parts take longer than others. The authors use another way of describing quantum algorithms that can handle branches. For a famous quantum search method, branches alone give a worse result than known before. When they also include loops, they match the earlier result. So it matters how you describe the flow of a program.

2604.01429v2.accessible: Classical shadows are a technique for efficiently predicting properties of an unknown quantum state from measurements. A common recipe is to measure the state in a randomly chosen basis, with the randomness coming from a symmetry group; many such recipes have been studied one at a time. The authors give a unified theory covering recipes based on general group representations (the ways a symmetry group can act on a quantum system), going beyond earlier simplified settings. They identify 'centralizing bases', which make the analysis exact and the classical post-processing cheap, and give general bounds on how many measurements are needed for a given precision. It also yields new protocols, for example based on the exceptional group G2.
2604.01429v2.simple: Scientists want to learn about an unknown quantum state. A method called classical shadows does this efficiently. It measures the state in a randomly chosen way. Many versions of this method exist, each studied on its own. The authors build one theory that covers many of them. It shows how to keep the computer work after measuring small. It also tells how many measurements you need. And it helps create new versions.

2603.21873v2.accessible: Quantum phase estimation is a standard quantum method for finding the lowest energy of a physical system, its 'ground state energy'. Its data must then be processed on an ordinary computer. The authors introduce a new classical estimator for the common case where the wanted value lies in a known interval. It filters the data to that interval, which makes it robust both to unwanted extra signals and to noise. They prove that without noise its systematic error (bias) shrinks exponentially compared with a simple average, and that it copes better with a common noise model. So far it has been tested only in a small simulation of a magnetic model, where it performed better than expected.
2603.21873v2.simple: Quantum computers may help find the lowest energy of a physical system. One method gives raw data that a normal computer must then process. The authors build a new way to process this data. It works when you roughly know where the answer is. By ignoring signals outside that range, it is less sensitive to noise and unwanted signals. So far it has only been tested in a small simulation on a normal computer, where it did better than expected.

2603.05391v1.accessible: Cat states, also called GHZ states, are entangled states of many qubits: a quantum superposition of 'all zeros' and 'all ones'. Preparing them 'fault-tolerantly', so that a few faults cannot spread into many errors, is an important step in quantum error correction. Earlier methods relied on expensive computer searches; the authors take a more scalable, constructive route. Using ZX-diagrams, a graphical language for quantum circuits, they reduce the problem to studying certain simple graphs and prove lower bounds on the number of two-qubit CNOT gates needed. They then find circuits matching these bounds for all cat states up to 50 qubits and nearly all up to 100, for the fault levels considered.
2603.05391v1.simple: Quantum computers make errors, so they need error correction. One helpful tool is a 'cat state', a special shared state of many qubits. It must be made carefully, so that a few small errors do not spread. Older methods used slow computer searches. The authors use a picture-based language for circuits to find the best recipes in a smarter way. They prove how many steps are needed. Then, for many sizes, they find recipes using exactly that many.

2602.08441v1.accessible: In the mathematics of symmetry, numbers called multiplicities count how often a basic building block appears inside a larger structure. Some, such as Kostka and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients, have a counting interpretation that places them in the complexity class #P, which captures counting problems. Whether this holds more widely is an important open question, relevant to geometric complexity theory and quantum information. The authors show that a broad class of these multiplicities, including the plethysm coefficients, lies in #BQP, a quantum counterpart of #P. This unifies, simplifies and extends earlier results. The proof uses repeated applications of the Schur transform, a quantum circuit tied to symmetry. They also give fast classical algorithms when certain parameters are fixed.
2602.08441v1.simple: In maths, some numbers count how often a basic piece of symmetry appears inside a bigger one. For some of these numbers, we know a neat way to count them. For many others, we do not. The authors show that a large group of these numbers can be counted, in a certain sense, with a quantum computer. This includes numbers called plethysm coefficients. Their result also covers earlier work. When some settings are fixed, normal computers can find them fast.

2601.21863v1.accessible: Quantum error-correcting codes protect information by spreading it over many qubits. The Bravyi-König theorem is an important 'no-go' result for topological stabiliser codes, a family of such codes: it limits which logical operations short, shallow circuits can perform, depending on the dimension of the code. A newer type, Floquet codes, uses repeated measurements to create the protected space anew at each time step. The authors prove that the Bravyi-König theorem also holds for Floquet codes, under a definition based on 'locally conjugate' stabiliser groups. They also define a broader class of operations that need not preserve the protected space at every step but, together with the measurements, still act validly, and prove the theorem holds for these too.
2601.21863v1.simple: Quantum computers need protection from errors. Error-correcting codes give this protection. An important rule says that, for one big family of codes, quick and simple operations can only do a limited set of things. A newer kind of code, called a Floquet code, keeps changing over time through repeated measurements. The authors show that the rule also applies to these new codes. It even applies to a wider set of operations that they define.

2602.00069v1.accessible: Quantum key distribution (QKD) lets two parties share secret keys without relying on assumptions about computing power, but current hardware limits it to fairly short distances. To go further, networks of trusted repeater nodes are used: QKD runs between neighbouring nodes, and messages are relayed through the network. Such networks are being deployed worldwide, yet no protocol had provable guarantees that messages cannot be tampered with, either by outside attackers or by corrupted nodes along the way. The authors present the first protocol that provably provides both secrecy and integrity. It combines Algebraic Manipulation Detection codes, an existing cryptographic tool for spotting tampering, with relaying messages along several paths, and its security is proven formally.
2602.00069v1.simple: Quantum key distribution lets two people share secret keys very safely. But it only works over short distances. To reach further, messages hop between trusted stations. Such networks are being built around the world. Until now, no method could prove that nobody changed a message along the way. The authors give the first method that keeps messages both secret and unchanged, with a mathematical proof. It sends messages along several routes and uses a special code that spots tampering.

2608.28569v2.accessible: The quantum Fourier transform is a key building block of many quantum algorithms. It can be defined not only for simple number systems but for general groups, including 'non-abelian' groups, where the order of operations matters. A standard example is the symmetric group: all the ways to reorder a list of items. A quantum circuit for this transform was outlined in 1997 and analysed in more detail in 2016. The authors revisit that construction, carefully recount its cost, and give revised estimates for the number of gates and the depth of the circuit. They also notice that one design choice in the earlier construction was not optimal, and propose a simpler way to build the transform.
2608.28569v2.simple: The quantum Fourier transform is an important tool used inside many quantum programs. It can be built for many kinds of mathematical structures. One of them describes all the ways to shuffle a list of items. A quantum circuit for this case was first sketched in 1997 and studied again in 2016. The authors check this circuit carefully. They give a corrected count of how many steps it needs. They also find a simpler way to build it.

2608.24494v1.accessible: Finding the lowest possible energy of a quantum system, its 'ground-state energy', is a central problem in physics and chemistry. Often one has a 'guiding state': a rough guess that partly overlaps with the true lowest-energy state. The usual approach lets the system evolve in time and estimates a property of the resulting operation, called an eigenphase. The authors design a quantum algorithm, with a mathematical proof, that needs fewer uses of this operation than the previous best method, saving more as the guess gets worse. This matches a known lower limit, so it cannot be improved, and answers an open question. It is built from 'transducers', which combine quantum algorithms without extra cost for error reduction.
2608.24494v1.simple: Scientists often want to know the lowest energy a molecule or material can have. Often they start with a rough guess of the answer. The authors design a new quantum method that uses this guess, and prove how well it works. It needs fewer runs of a key step than the best earlier method. It matches a known limit, so no method can do better. It joins smaller quantum programs together without wasting effort on reducing errors.

2608.20476v1.accessible: In a quantum walk, a quantum state spreads over a network, or graph. 'Perfect state transfer' happens when the state moves exactly from one node to another. Many examples use Cayley graphs, networks built from a mathematical group. The authors argue that state transfer belongs to the graph, not the group. They show that the constructions in six earlier papers, based on 'non-abelian' groups where the order of operations matters, in fact describe graphs that also come from simpler 'abelian' groups. They then give what is, to their knowledge, the first infinite family of such graphs with perfect state transfer that come from no abelian group, and list small symmetric examples up to 30 nodes.
2608.20476v1.simple: Imagine a network of points joined by lines. In a quantum walk, a quantum signal moves through this network. Sometimes the signal arrives perfectly at another point. Many such networks are built from patterns of symmetry. The authors show that many known examples really come from simple patterns, even though they looked complicated. They also find a whole family of networks where this is not the case. Finally, they list all small examples.

2607.28873v1.accessible: Beams of atoms that are continuous, dense and well aligned ('collimated') are useful for precise measurement and for depositing materials, and have been important for cold-atom experiments. Standard methods narrow the beam with laser light pushing equally from opposite sides, but at high atom densities the atoms absorb light unevenly and this balance breaks down. The authors introduce a different scheme. One laser transition, covering a broad range of frequencies, shifts the speeds of atoms, while a second, very narrow transition picks out atoms with the right speed. Selected atoms are 'shelved' in a long-lived internal state, which reduces light scattering and marks them as collimated. Simulations with strontium show effective collimation, and lab experiments agree well with them.
2607.28873v1.simple: Some experiments need a steady stream of atoms all flying in the same direction. Usually, laser light pushing evenly from both sides straightens the stream. When the stream is dense, this works badly. The authors use two kinds of laser light instead. One changes the speed of the atoms. The other picks out atoms with the right speed and stores them. Computer simulations and lab tests with strontium atoms agree that it works well.

2607.15358v1.accessible: Estimating the lowest energy of the electrons in a molecule or material, its 'ground-state energy', is a major quantum computing target. Here electrons are described in 'first quantization', using a spatial grid. The authors use a technique called sum-of-squares spectral gap amplification: they rewrite the energy operator as a sum of squared terms, built from the total charge density. This gives a guaranteed lower bound and a cheaper way to load the operator into a quantum circuit (a 'block encoding'). As a result, quantum phase estimation, the standard energy-estimation routine, provably needs fewer gates. For example systems, calculated resources fall by a factor of 2 to 44, the lowest yet for such materials simulations; nothing was run on hardware.
2607.15358v1.simple: Quantum computers may one day help us understand how electrons behave in molecules and materials. A key task is finding the lowest energy of these electrons. The authors find a smarter way to write down this energy, as a sum of squared parts. On paper, this makes the quantum calculation cheaper. For several example materials and molecules, the estimated cost drops by between 2 and 44 times. These are the lowest cost estimates so far.

2607.11217v2.accessible: Chemical processes play out on many scales at once, from electrons to whole reactors. Quantum algorithms have been proposed for each scale, but there is no systematic way to link them. The authors match four known quantum algorithms to four scales and ask when a quantum speed-up at each scale might survive these links. They stress that such speed-ups are not guaranteed: they depend on preparing inputs, memory design, numerical properties and the cost of reading out results. Using the oxidation of carbon monoxide on a platinum surface as an example, they set out six open questions and suggest that how information passes between scales mainly decides any overall advantage.
2607.11217v2.simple: Chemistry happens at many sizes at once. Tiny electrons, atoms, bigger groups of molecules and whole reactors all matter. There are quantum computer methods for each size. But nobody knows how to join them well. The authors match a quantum method to each size. They explain that a speed-up is not guaranteed. They list six open questions, using a reaction on platinum as an example. They suggest that how information passes between sizes matters most.

2605.26983v1.accessible: Quantum operations, called unitaries, can be sorted into a series of levels known as the Clifford hierarchy. The task studied here is testing: given an unknown operation, decide whether it is close to a chosen level. An earlier proposal linked this to quantum versions of 'uniformity norms', mathematical measures that detect hidden structure, but how efficient that test is remained unknown. The authors describe which operations come close to the largest possible value of the fourth such norm. As a consequence, they obtain an efficient test for the third level of the hierarchy. They also discuss possible routes to testing higher levels and the main obstacles that remain.
2605.26983v1.simple: Quantum computers carry out operations on data. These operations can be sorted into levels, a bit like floors of a building. The question is: given an unknown operation, can we check which level it is close to? An earlier idea suggested a test for this, but nobody knew how well it worked. The authors prove that the test works efficiently for the third level. They also explain what still blocks a test for higher levels.

2605.03023v1.accessible: 'Unitary designs' are operations that imitate truly random ones well enough for many quantum tasks, and 'strong' designs are a stricter version of this idea. Earlier work showed how to build strong designs on a line of qubits, or when every qubit can interact with every other. The authors build them on grids of two, three or more dimensions, where qubits only interact with their neighbours. One construction combines the all-to-all result with routing techniques and works for any layout, though slightly less efficiently. A second, direct construction needs no extra helper qubits and has the best possible circuit depth on grids. Combining the two, they also obtain 'pseudorandom' operations on grids with optimal depth.
2605.03023v1.simple: Many quantum tasks need operations that look random. Making them is not easy. In real quantum chips, each qubit can often only talk to its neighbours on a grid. Earlier work showed how to make such operations on a line of qubits. The authors show mathematically how to do it on flat grids and grids with more dimensions. One method works for any layout. Another method is proven to be as fast as possible on grids.

2603.29809v1.accessible: A Hamiltonian describes the energy of a quantum system and how it changes over time. The authors study 'local' Hamiltonians, where each term involves only a few particles, and ask how to check (certify) or learn them. First, they certify a Hamiltonian by letting the system evolve, using a total evolution time that is provably optimal; to their knowledge this is the first optimal test of a Hamiltonian property. Second, they learn 'Gibbs states', the states a system settles into at a given temperature, with an efficient number of samples, whereas earlier methods needed exponentially many samples at low temperatures. Third, they certify Gibbs states efficiently in both samples and running time, answering an open question from 2022.
2603.29809v1.simple: Physicists describe a quantum system by a rule for its energy. The authors ask how to check or learn this rule from measurements. They design methods and analyse them mathematically. One checks the rule in as little time as possible. Another learns the state a system settles into at a given temperature. Earlier methods needed far too many measurements when the system is cold. The new method does not.

2603.10981v1.accessible: Quantum error-correcting codes protect information by spreading it over many physical units. In permutation-invariant codes, the encoded states stay the same when the physical units are swapped around. The authors study such codes for qubits and for 'qudits', units with more than two levels, focusing on deletion errors, where units are lost. They extend the standard conditions for error correction to qudits and search numerically for codes. They conjecture a minimum number of qubits needed to correct a given number of deletions, and find that using physical qudits with more levels steadily reduces the number of units needed, approaching a known theoretical limit. They also extend an existing construction to qudits by solving a linear program.
2603.10981v1.simple: Quantum information is easily damaged. Error-correcting codes protect it by spreading it over many small parts. The authors study codes that do not change when the parts are shuffled. They look at parts with two levels and parts with more levels. Using computer searches, they guess how many parts are needed to recover from lost parts. They find that parts with more levels mean fewer parts are needed. They also give a new way to build such codes.

2602.20900v1.accessible: Quantum error-correcting codes protect information by spreading it across many qubits. The authors study 'brickwork' circuits: layers of random operations on neighbouring pairs of qubits along a line, arranged like bricks in a wall, using a restricted class of operations called Clifford gates. They prove that, on average, these circuits form good approximate error-correcting codes after a number of layers that grows only logarithmically with the number of qubits. The proof adapts statistical-mechanics methods developed earlier for studying random circuits. For exact error correction, where no error at all is allowed, they give matching upper and lower bounds on the number of layers needed before such circuits become error-correcting.
2602.20900v1.simple: Quantum information breaks easily, so it needs protection. One way to protect it is to spread it over many qubits in a clever pattern. The authors look at a simple random circuit. The qubits sit in a line and are mixed in a pattern like bricks in a wall. They prove that this random mixing protects information well after relatively few layers. They also find how many layers are needed for perfect protection.

2602.06114v3.accessible: Quantum systems of many particles, pushed far from equilibrium, can show phase transitions, chaos and entanglement, but these are hard to study in large, well-isolated systems. The Dicke model, in which many two-level systems all couple to a single mode of light or vibration, is a basic picture of how light and matter interact. The authors realise this model with a flat crystal of about 100 trapped ions, whose shared vibration plays the role of the mode. They observe dynamical phase transitions between ordered and disordered spin phases, signs of chaos, and behaviour consistent with quantum thermalisation. Calculations, supported by measurements, indicate quantum correlations ('squeezing') 2.6 dB below the standard quantum limit, a resource for quantum-enhanced sensing.
2602.06114v3.simple: Physicists want to know how many particles behave together when pushed out of balance. A well-known model describes many tiny 'switches' that all share one vibration. It is a simple picture of light meeting matter. The authors recreate this model in the lab with about 100 charged atoms held in a flat crystal. They see the system switch between different behaviours, signs of chaos, and settling down. They also find quantum correlations that could help make better sensors.

2601.21553v2.accessible: Tensors, multi-dimensional arrays of numbers, appear across computer science, mathematics and quantum information. Strassen's 'asymptotic spectrum' is a framework for measuring how complex tensors are, using special measures called spectral points. A question open since 1991 asked whether Strassen's 'support functionals' are such universal spectral points. The authors answer yes for tensors over the complex numbers, by showing that these functionals equal the 'quantum functionals', which are defined by optimising entropy over sets linked to entanglement. This follows from a general formula that acts as a bridge between classical and quantum versions of a problem. The results also give a simpler, unified approach to several other tensor measures.
2601.21553v2.simple: Tensors are tables of numbers that can have many directions, not just rows and columns. They appear in computer science, mathematics and quantum physics. A well-known question from 1991 asked whether certain ways of measuring tensors have a special property. The authors prove that the answer is yes. They show that these measures are the same as other measures that come from quantum physics. Their method also makes several other results simpler.
